governing_spec.title: vllm-oxide v0.2.0 — trustworthy single-GPU inference and release closure
governing_spec.body:
## Problem Statement

v0.1 proves that the Rust/CUDA stack can load Qwen3 weights, execute paged attention, schedule requests, sample tokens, and compare selected outputs against Python-generated golden fixtures. The current implementation, however, does not yet provide a trustworthy release baseline for real offline generation.

Several correctness invariants are distributed across `LLM`, `EngineCore`, `Scheduler`, `Sequence`, `KVCacheManager`, attention metadata construction, and the sampler rather than being expressed through one schedulable unit of work. As a result, repeated use of one `LLM` instance can lose outputs, chunked prefill can sample before the prompt is complete, prefix-cached prefill can use inconsistent token and KV lengths, recompute-only preemption can omit generated history, and a batch can exceed the configured token budget. Some cache and no-progress failures are also ignored, which creates a risk of silent hangs or placeholder outputs.

The request contract is similarly incomplete: `SamplingParams` fields accepted by the public API are not all preserved through scheduling and execution, invalid combinations are not consistently rejected, and EOS handling is tied to a fixed token rather than resolved model/tokenizer metadata. On the GPU hot path, sampling copies full vocabulary rows to the CPU, while attention metadata is repeatedly materialized instead of being prepared once per engine step. Model initialization can resolve the same artifacts more than once, disregard the requested dtype, temporarily allocate duplicate KV caches, and call synchronization a warmup without exercising a real forward path.

The existing validation and release workflow can report success without validating the complete product contract. Fixture discovery can omit batch and regression cases, oracle failures can still exit successfully, empty comparison sets can pass vacuously, L1 near-tie handling is ineffective for actual mismatches, and L2 comparison does not consistently stop at the first divergent token. The published golden release layout also differs from the downloader contract, the documented CUDA CLI command does not match the crate feature surface, and there is no formal v0.1.0 GitHub release to establish a repeatable precedent.

v0.2.0 therefore needs to be a hardening release: a trustworthy, repeatable, and releasable single-GPU Qwen3 offline inference engine whose behavior is demonstrated at the public API seam and whose GPU correctness gate fails closed.

## Solution

Make v0.2.0 a correctness-first release centered on one public behavioral seam and one internal scheduling seam.

The public behavioral seam remains `LLM::generate`. Every supported user-visible requirement—request identity, batching, repeated calls, sampling, EOS, prefix reuse, chunked prefill, preemption, errors, and output order—must be observable and testable through that interface.

Internally, deepen the engine module around a single immutable `StepPlan` produced by the scheduler and a corresponding `StepResult` returned after execution. A plan identifies exactly which sequences participate in a step, the token ranges and positions to execute, the prefill/decode phase, whether each sequence may sample, and the cache/attention metadata needed for that work. `EngineCore` executes only the plan; it does not rediscover work by traversing mutable scheduler state. The scheduler remains the sole owner of sequence lifecycle, token-budget accounting, cache allocation, prefix-cache accounting, preemption, progress detection, and application of step results.

Complete the accepted single-GPU product contract before expanding scope: preserve and validate all supported sampling parameters, resolve model artifacts and metadata once, create one correctly sized KV cache, perform a real warmup, keep sampling and step metadata device-resident where practical, and expose only the small public API needed for offline generation.

Replace permissive validation with a fail-closed golden and release pipeline. The reference oracle is authoritative for correctness, the vLLM oracle is calibration evidence, every declared fixture must be discovered and classified, comparison must use sound same-prefix semantics, and any generation, discovery, comparison, or coverage failure must make the release gate fail. The documented Quick Start, CUDA build, quality checks, golden asset contract, changelog, tag, and GitHub release must all describe the same versioned product.

## User Stories

1. As a library user, I can construct an `LLM` for a supported Qwen3 causal language model and generate text on one CUDA device using the documented API.
2. As a library user, I can call `LLM::generate` at least 100 times on the same instance without outputs being dropped, replaced by placeholders, or associated with stale sequence identifiers.
3. As a library user, I receive exactly one `RequestOutput` for every accepted prompt, in the same order as the input prompts, even when internal scheduling order differs.
4. As a library user, I can distinguish requests by stable request identity without depending on an internal sequence identifier being a dense batch index.
5. As a library user, I can submit mixed prompt lengths in one call and receive complete outputs for short and long prompts without one request corrupting another request's state.
6. As a library user, I can supply per-prompt sampling settings, and each request retains its own settings throughout its lifetime.
7. As a library user, supported temperature, top-k, top-p, presence penalty, frequency penalty, repetition penalty, maximum-token, and EOS behavior are actually applied rather than silently replaced by defaults.
8. As a library user, invalid sampling settings and unsupported combinations are rejected before execution with an actionable error.
9. As a library user, greedy generation is deterministic for the same resolved model revision, prompt, options, and golden environment.
10. As a library user, generation stops on the EOS token resolved from the model/tokenizer contract unless `ignore_eos` is set, and never relies on a model-specific hard-coded constant.
11. As a library user, reaching `max_tokens` has a clear and consistent meaning independent of prompt length, prefix-cache hits, and preemption.
12. As a library user, an internal allocation, scheduling, model, attention, or sampling failure is returned as a contextual error instead of becoming an empty output or an indefinite loop.
13. As a library user, the supported public surface is small and stable: model source and engine options in, prompts and sampling parameters in, request outputs or errors out.
14. As an operator, I can request a supported dtype and know that the loaded model, kernels, and cache use the validated dtype or fail explicitly.
15. As an operator, a remote model resolves to one immutable revision for configuration, tokenizer, and weights during an `LLM` lifetime.
16. As an operator, initialization fetches or resolves each model artifact once rather than independently resolving the same moving branch multiple times.
17. As an operator, initialization creates one KV-cache allocation derived from the configured memory budget and does not temporarily retain a second model-owned cache of a different size.
18. As an operator, warmup executes a representative model path and surfaces CUDA, shape, dtype, and kernel incompatibilities before the first user request.
19. As an operator, configured memory limits fail early with a useful capacity error when the requested cache cannot be allocated safely.
20. As a scheduler maintainer, every engine step is represented by one immutable `StepPlan` containing only the sequences and tokens that are scheduled for that step.
21. As a scheduler maintainer, a `StepPlan` explicitly distinguishes prefill from decode and explicitly states whether sampling is allowed for each scheduled sequence.
22. As a scheduler maintainer, the configured maximum number of batched tokens is enforced across the whole step, not only for the first sequence considered.
23. As a scheduler maintainer, waiting requests can be admitted while other requests are decoding when token and cache budgets permit, providing actual continuous batching rather than admission only when the running set becomes empty.
24. As a scheduler maintainer, fairness and progress rules prevent a runnable request from starving indefinitely behind a long-running request.
25. As a scheduler maintainer, a sequence with zero scheduled tokens is never sent through model execution and cannot trigger index underflow or stale-state reads.
26. As a scheduler maintainer, every successful step consumes tokens, changes lifecycle state, or completes work; otherwise the engine returns an explicit no-progress error.
27. As a scheduler maintainer, cache allocation and release failures are propagated and leave sequence/cache ownership in a consistent state.
28. As a chunked-prefill user, a long prompt can be processed over multiple steps without sampling or appending completion tokens until its final prompt chunk has completed.
29. As a prefix-caching user, cached prompt tokens are excluded from new model input while their KV entries remain correctly visible to attention with consistent positions and lengths.
30. As a prefix-caching user, a batch can mix full cache hits, partial cache hits, and cache misses without cross-request corruption.
31. As a preemption user, recompute-only preemption reconstructs the complete causal history required to resume a request, including generated completion tokens, not only the original prompt.
32. As an engine maintainer, execution applies a `StepResult` back to scheduler-owned state exactly once, so token advancement, sampling, completion, and cache changes cannot be duplicated.
33. As an engine maintainer, attention metadata is prepared once per step in the form needed by the CUDA path rather than rebuilt independently by each layer or sequence.
34. As a performance user, normal decode does not copy a full vocabulary-sized logits row from GPU to CPU for every request and token.
35. As a performance user, only the minimal data needed for API output crosses from GPU to CPU after device-side sampling.
36. As a correctness maintainer, every declared canonical, batch, and regression golden fixture is discovered, loaded, and compared, with unmatched or skipped fixtures reported as failures.
37. As a correctness maintainer, a reference-oracle generation failure exits non-zero and cannot leave a partial fixture set that is later presented as complete.
38. As a correctness maintainer, an empty comparison set, missing manifest entry, missing asset, or unsupported fixture shape fails closed instead of passing vacuously.
39. As a correctness maintainer, the Transformers SDPA reference oracle defines expected correctness, while the vLLM baseline oracle is used for calibration and investigation rather than as a second independent pass/fail truth.
40. As a correctness maintainer, L1 near-tie handling is based on a sound comparison of candidate logits and can classify a genuine numerically ambiguous mismatch without circular top-1 assumptions.
41. As a correctness maintainer, L2 compares only the same generated prefix and stops at the first divergent token, so later logits are never compared under different causal histories.
42. As a correctness maintainer, numerical tolerances are derived, documented, versioned, and justified by dtype/kernel evidence rather than increased until tests pass.
43. As a release engineer, the golden publisher and downloader share one documented asset layout, checksum policy, manifest schema, and version naming convention.
44. As a release engineer, the production CUDA feature path builds and runs through the same supported CLI command shown in the Quick Start.
45. As a release engineer, Rust formatting, linting, tests, dependency policy, and MSRV checks pass, and Python tests, Ruff, and mypy checks pass for the golden tooling.
46. As a release engineer, the GPU release gate executes the complete generation and golden comparison workflow and cannot succeed after a skipped phase or swallowed exception.
47. As a release engineer, v0.2.0 has aligned crate versions, documentation, changelog entries, a `v0.2.0` tag, a formal GitHub release, and a compatible `goldens-v0.2` asset release.
48. As a new user, I can copy the documented Quick Start command on a supported CUDA host and complete one deterministic generation without discovering undocumented features or setup steps.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Product boundary:** v0.2.0 supports offline causal text generation for the existing Qwen3 model family on one CUDA device. Correctness and release closure take priority over new model families or serving features.
- **Highest test seam:** `LLM::generate` is the authoritative behavioral seam. Lower-level tests support diagnosis, but no collection of component tests substitutes for end-to-end behavior at this interface.
- **Internal engine seam:** scheduling produces an immutable `StepPlan`; execution returns a `StepResult`. This is the only coordination seam between scheduler-owned mutable state and model execution.
- **Plan contents:** each plan identifies scheduled request/sequence identity, phase, exact token range, logical positions, cache block mapping, attention lengths, token budget contribution, and whether sampling is permitted. It cannot implicitly include every currently running sequence.
- **Scheduler ownership:** `Scheduler` owns request lifecycle, admission, fairness, global token-budget accounting, prefix-cache accounting, recompute-only preemption, completion, and progress detection. `EngineCore` must not infer these decisions by traversing scheduler collections.
- **Cache ownership:** `KVCacheManager` and `BlockPool` remain internal structural adapters behind the scheduler. Allocation and deallocation are transactional from the scheduler's perspective, and all failures are returned.
- **Prefill contract:** uncached prompt ranges and cached KV ranges are represented separately. Sampling is legal only after all prompt tokens for a request are represented in the causal state.
- **Preemption contract:** recompute-only preemption discards physical cache residency but preserves the logical request history necessary to rebuild prompt and generated-token KV state.
- **Request identity:** public request ordering and identity are independent of monotonic internal sequence identifiers. Reusing an `LLM` instance never assumes that sequence identifiers start at zero for a call.
- **Sampling contract:** one validated `SamplingParams` value follows each request throughout scheduling and execution. Supported fields cannot be silently discarded. Model/tokenizer metadata supplies EOS behavior.
- **Device hot path:** filtering, penalties, probability selection, and token choice remain on the device where supported. Full vocabulary rows are not copied to the host during normal decode.
- **Attention preparation:** an internal attention context converts plan metadata into device-ready metadata once per step and reuses it across the model layers participating in that step. The existing CUDA paged-attention implementation is the only runtime backend required for v0.2.0; no premature backend trait is introduced.
- **Model artifacts:** a resolved-model object binds source, immutable revision, configuration, tokenizer, weights, dtype, and special-token metadata once. All model construction consumes this resolved identity.
- **Initialization:** cache sizing occurs once after model configuration and available memory are known. Warmup performs real representative work without mutating user-visible request state.
- **Public API depth:** only the composition-root API and its input/output types are public. Scheduler, sequence, cache, attention, model-loader, and sampler mechanics remain private unless an independently useful public contract is demonstrated.
- **Oracle roles:** the reference oracle is the source of expected values. The baseline oracle supplies calibration evidence. The two roles are not combined into an ambiguous double pass/fail gate.
- **Golden contract:** fixture families, manifest coverage, comparison level, dtype, model revision, kernel/runtime versions, tolerances, asset checksums, and generator version are explicit release metadata.
- **Fail-closed release behavior:** discovery, generation, download, validation, comparison, and coverage checks return non-zero on any error. Skips are allowed only when explicitly declared as non-release exploratory behavior and can never satisfy the release gate.
- **Versioning:** the code release and golden release use compatible but distinct names: `v0.2.0` for the product and `goldens-v0.2` for its fixture assets.
- **Tensor parallelism seam:** v0.2.0 may document a feasibility decision for the existing TP-oriented abstractions, but runtime TP/NCCL implementation is not part of this release and dead hooks must not be presented as supported behavior.

## Testing Decisions

- Add black-box tests at `LLM::generate` for a single prompt, mixed-length batches, per-prompt sampling, input/output ordering, EOS, invalid parameters, contextual failures, and at least 100 sequential calls on one `LLM` instance.
- Add deterministic scheduler contract tests around `StepPlan` and `StepResult`: global token-budget enforcement, exact sequence membership, no zero-token work, admission during decode, fairness, progress, chunk boundaries, cache allocation failure, completion, and result application exactly once.
- Add scenario tests for no cache hit, full prefix hit, partial prefix hit, mixed hits in one batch, multi-step chunked prefill, decode under KV pressure, recompute-only preemption after generated tokens exist, and recovery to the same deterministic output as an unpreempted run.
- Add assertions that an incomplete prefill plan cannot sample and that every sampled sequence has completed prompt ingestion.
- Add model-initialization tests for immutable revision reuse, requested dtype propagation, special-token resolution, a single cache allocation, capacity errors, and a real warmup failure path.
- Add structural/performance checks showing that normal decode performs no full-vocabulary device-to-host transfer and that attention metadata is materialized once per step. Record prefill throughput, decode throughput, time to first token, per-token latency, and peak memory on the release GPU as versioned evidence; use structural regressions as hard failures and hardware-specific timing deltas as reviewed release evidence.
- Generate and compare every fixture named by the release manifest across canonical, batch, and regression families. The gate must report exact totals for expected, discovered, generated, compared, skipped, and failed fixtures; release acceptance requires zero missing, zero unexpected, zero skipped, and zero failed fixtures.
- L1 acceptance requires the expected next token or an explicitly justified near-tie classification computed from the same-prefix candidate logits. Near-tie policy and thresholds must be recorded in the manifest.
- L2 acceptance compares reference and Rust logits only while token prefixes match, reports the first divergence, and stops that case immediately. It must not compare later steps from different prefixes.
- The legacy broad tolerance is not an acceptance baseline. v0.2.0 must root-cause the observed error distribution and establish per-dtype/per-kernel tolerances from calibration evidence before the release gate is considered trustworthy.
- Oracle generation, fixture publication, asset download, manifest validation, Rust execution, and report generation each have explicit non-zero failure behavior. Tests cover partial output, malformed metadata, missing archives/assets, checksum mismatch, and empty inputs.
- CPU CI remains responsible for `cargo fmt --check`, Clippy with warnings denied, Rust unit/integration/doc tests that do not require CUDA, Python tests, Ruff, mypy, dependency-policy checks, and the declared MSRV.
- A GPU release job is responsible for the production CUDA build, actual model warmup, public API scenarios, complete golden comparison, and the documented CLI smoke test. A CPU-only green build cannot substitute for this job.
- Release acceptance requires the Quick Start command to work unchanged on the documented environment, the CLI feature contract to match that command, all version strings to agree, all release assets to be downloadable by the shipped tooling, and both `v0.2.0` and `goldens-v0.2` releases to exist.

## Out of Scope

- Tensor parallel execution, NCCL collectives, multi-GPU scheduling, or claiming the existing TP seam as production-ready.
- CUDA Graph capture, speculative decoding, quantization, LoRA, and other throughput features that add new correctness dimensions.
- Async APIs, an HTTP server, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, streaming responses, distributed serving, or production autoscaling.
- Additional model families, embedding/classification tasks, multimodal inputs, or tokenizer families beyond what the supported Qwen3 contract requires.
- L3 internal-activation golden fixtures; v0.2.0 closes the L1 token and L2 logits contracts first.
- Broad public exposure of internal scheduler, cache, attention, loader, model, or sampler implementation types.
- Hard cross-hardware latency promises. v0.2.0 records a reproducible baseline and removes known structural hot-path regressions without claiming universal performance parity with vLLM.

## Further Notes

- This is the parent implementation specification for v0.2.0. Delivery should be decomposed into dependency-ordered tickets without reopening the product boundary or the two accepted seams.
- Recommended delivery order:
  1. Establish red behavioral tests, fixture coverage accounting, and reproducible performance evidence for the current failure modes.
  2. Introduce the `StepPlan` / `StepResult` engine seam and correct repeated calls, token budgeting, continuous admission, chunked prefill, prefix caching, progress handling, and recompute-only preemption.
  3. Complete sampling semantics, request validation/identity, resolved model artifacts, dtype propagation, special-token resolution, single cache allocation, and real warmup.
  4. Make GPU sampling and attention-step metadata device-oriented, then close full fail-closed golden validation and tolerance calibration.
  5. Minimize the public API, repair the CLI and quality gates, declare MSRV, update documentation/changelog, and publish the product and golden releases.
- The current repository is a strong v0.1 architectural prototype with a passing Rust test suite; the objective here is not a rewrite. The deep engine seam concentrates existing responsibilities so their invariants can be tested and trusted.
- A short TP feasibility spike may end in an ADR that either preserves, revises, or removes currently unused TP-oriented hooks. Any runtime TP implementation should be planned for a later release after the single-GPU contract is stable.

acceptance_obligations: A StepPlan explicitly identifies scheduled request and sequence identity, phase, exact token ranges, logical positions, token-budget contribution, cache and attention metadata, and whether sampling is permitted.
EngineCore executes only sequences present in the StepPlan and no longer discovers work by traversing the Scheduler running set.

## Parent

- #28

## What to build

Introduce the accepted internal engine seam without expanding the public API. Scheduler-owned mutable state produces an immutable StepPlan, EngineCore executes only that plan, and a StepResult is applied back to scheduler state exactly once. Preserve the currently supported single-request and batched greedy-generation behavior while making later correctness work local to this seam.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A StepPlan explicitly identifies scheduled request and sequence identity, phase, exact token ranges, logical positions, token-budget contribution, cache and attention metadata, and whether sampling is permitted.
- [ ] EngineCore executes only sequences present in the StepPlan and no longer discovers work by traversing the Scheduler running set.
- [ ] Applying a StepResult advances token, lifecycle, completion, and cache state exactly once; stale or duplicate application is rejected.
- [ ] Plans cannot silently contain zero-token work or unscheduled running sequences.
- [ ] Existing supported prefill, decode, and batched greedy-generation tests remain green through the new seam.
- [ ] Focused contract tests make StepPlan and StepResult behavior deterministic without requiring CUDA.

## Blocked by

- None (can start immediately).
